steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Key ways in which ribonucleic acid (RNA) and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) differ:

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA contains deoxyribose (lacks an –OH group on the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA contains ribose (has an –OH on the 2′ carbon).  
   → The extra hydroxyl makes RNA more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), thymine (T).  
   • RNA: A, G, C, uracil (U) replaces thymine.  
   → Uracil is energetically cheaper to synthesize; thymine’s methyl group helps DNA error-checking and stability.

3. Strandedness & shape  
   • DNA is usually double-stranded, forming a long antiparallel double helix (B-form in cells).  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded and folds into complex 3-D shapes (hairpins, loops, pseudoknots). Some viruses carry double-stranded RNA.

4. Length & quantity  
   • DNA molecules are typically very long (chromosomes, plasmids) and few in number.  
   • Cells make many short RNA molecules (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, miRNA, etc.) in large quantities and turn them over rapidly.

5. Location in eukaryotic cells  
   • DNA primarily stays in the nucleus (and mitochondria/chloroplasts).  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus (or organelles) but functions mostly in the cytoplasm; some RNAs also work in the nucleus and other compartments.

6. Stability & lifespan  
   • DNA is chemically and enzymatically stable—persists for the life of the cell (or organism).  
   • RNA is comparatively unstable—degraded in minutes to hours; rapid turnover allows dynamic gene regulation.

7. Functions  
   • DNA: long-term storage of genetic information; template for its own replication; heredity.  
   • RNA: diverse functional roles  
     – Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries coding information for proteins.  
     – Transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA) are essential for translation.  
     – Regulatory RNAs (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA, etc.) control gene expression.  
     – Catalytic RNAs (ribozymes) perform enzymatic reactions (e.g., peptidyl transferase in ribosome).  
     – Some viruses use RNA as their genetic material.

8. Replication vs. transcription  
   • DNA is duplicated by DNA polymerases before cell division.  
   • RNA is synthesized (transcribed) from a DNA template using RNA polymerases; most RNA is not replicated.

9. Repair mechanisms  
   • DNA has elaborate repair systems (mismatch repair, base-excision, nucleotide-excision, recombination repair).  
   • RNA rarely repaired; instead it is usually degraded and resynthesized.

10. Chemical modifications  
    • DNA modifications: methylation of cytosine/adenine for epigenetic regulation.  
    • RNA modifications: >150 known (m6A, pseudouridine, 2′-O-methylation) important for stability, splicing, translation.

In short: DNA is a durable, double-stranded repository of genetic information; RNA is a versatile, single-stranded working copy that conveys, regulates, or sometimes catalyzes biological processes.
